metadata.title: Claude, Compared.
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Swedish. Wagwan check: charsum('claude-liam-llm-apis-compared') % 10 == 8, not 0.
metadata.note: deep-explainer comparing the four major LLM APIs -- OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google -- on the user's requested axes (cost, context window, use case, open-source/proprietary) plus two volunteered axes (deployment model, and the 2026 licensing shift). No book chapter this time -- all figures researched live this session via the claude-api skill (Anthropic, cached 2026-10-06) and direct WebFetch of each vendor's own official pricing/docs pages (OpenAI: developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing + /models; Google: ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing + /models; Meta: dev.meta.ai), not from training-data memory or third-party aggregator sites (several of which returned conflicting numbers and were explicitly rejected as sources -- see FACTCHECK.md). All pricing is flagged as perishable/current-as-of-date, per this session's standing discipline. 4 acts: I cost (official per-token pricing across all four, plus the structural point that open-weight models have no vendor-set price), II context window (the ~1M-token convergence across flagships, and what still varies -- output caps and shared-vs-separate counting), III use case (each company's real specialization, framed as a deliberate bet, not a ranking), IV open vs. proprietary (the old clean split vs. the 2026 reality: Meta's own lineup now runs both a closed frontier model and a true open-weight one). No Manim on this machine (pangocairo not installed) -- MANIM lane absorbed into REMOTION. VOX quota: 5 real Wikimedia Commons photographs, metaphor imagery. BinaryBranch/DivergentFates hero beats planned up front at A1-5, A2-4, A3-5, A4-4 (one per act) for clean 9:16 Short derivation. Signed for Divyank from authoring time, including the outro card. GATE P: PENDING, see PEDAGOGY.md.

beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Hej — this is Liam, in for Divyank. Four companies, four different bets on what a language model A-P-I should cost, hold, and be built for. Let's actually compare them — cost, context window, use case, and the open-versus-closed question that just got a lot more complicated.

show.event: composer cold-opens, spark + 'Hej, Liam' greeting settles
command types itself in: the four-way API comparison

props.command: Compare the four major LLM APIs — OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google — on cost, context window, use case, and open versus proprietary weights, with current official pricing.
output: three hyperscalers now price in the same rough band
the context-window race has basically converged, near 1M tokens
the open-vs-closed split just got messier, not simpler

beats.act: Act I — What Each Token Actually Costs
beats.narration_text: A price posted before you buy, metered exactly to what you used — that's how three of these four companies sell access to their models. Pay per token, in and out, no separate bill for the hardware underneath.

beats.act: Act I — What Each Token Actually Costs
beats.narration_text: Anthropic's current lineup, per million tokens: Opus five-point-five at four dollars in, twenty out. Sonnet five-point-five at two and ten. Haiku five-point-five at ten cents and fifty cents.

beats.act: Act I — What Each Token Actually Costs
beats.narration_text: OpenAI's current lineup, per million tokens: their top short-context model at ten dollars in, fifty out. The mid-tier at two and ten. The budget tier at ten cents and fifty cents — the same floor Anthropic lands on.

props.caption: official OpenAI rates, current as of Oct. 2026

beats.act: Act I — What Each Token Actually Costs
beats.narration_text: No meter here at all. You work the handle, you get the water — the infrastructure is yours, so there's no per-use bill from the company that designed it in the first place.

beats.act: Act I — What Each Token Actually Costs
beats.narration_text: Proprietary access is a fixed, published price per token, set by the vendor, the same for everyone. Open weights have no such price — download the model, and the cost becomes whatever your own hardware, or whichever host you pick, actually charges you.

beats.act: Act I — What Each Token Actually Costs
beats.narration_text: Google's current flagship, per million tokens: two dollars in, ten out — through the end of November 2026. Starting December first, that rises to four and twenty. A scheduled price increase, stated on their own pricing page.

beats.narration_text: Act two: the context window race.

beats.act: Act II — The Context Window Race
beats.narration_text: How much can one vessel actually hold before it sails? Stack enough containers and the number stops being the interesting question — everyone's hull is roughly the same size now.

shot.prompt: real photo of a container ship stacked high with cargo containers in port -- illustrative of raw holding capacity, not a literal depiction of a context window. Already sourced, see media/A2-1.source.txt

beats.act: Act II — The Context Window Race
beats.narration_text: Anthropic's current flagships — Opus five-point-five, Sonnet five-point-five, Fable five-point-one — all share a one-million-token context window, with a hundred-twenty-eight-thousand-token output cap.

props.caption: the same window across Opus, Sonnet, and Fable 5.1

beats.act: Act II — The Context Window Race
beats.narration_text: OpenAI's current flagships cluster at roughly one-point-oh-five million tokens of context, also capped at a hundred-twenty-eight-thousand tokens of output — the same shape, independently arrived at.

props.caption: the same shape, a different company

beats.act: Act II — The Context Window Race
beats.narration_text: One million tokens can go two different ways. Spend it on input, and you hand the model an entire codebase at once. Spend it on output, and a hundred-twenty-eight-thousand-token ceiling still caps how much it can actually hand back.

show.event: two tracks diverge: input capacity, output ceiling

beats.act: Act II — The Context Window Race
beats.narration_text: Google's current flagship states a shared one-million-token window, covering both input and output together — a different accounting choice than counting them separately, even at a similar total size.

items: 1M tokens, stated as a shared input+output window
props.caption: a different way of counting the same rough size

beats.act: Act II — The Context Window Race
beats.narration_text: The race converged. A few years ago, context size was the headline spec. Now three separate companies all cluster near one million tokens — it stopped being the thing that tells them apart.

props.sparkLine: Why this stopped being the differentiator.
items: the real variation now: output caps, and how the window is counted
props.caption: size converged. the counting didn't

beats.narration_text: Act three: built for what, exactly.

beats.act: Act III — Built For What, Exactly
beats.narration_text: One handle, several distinct blades — each shaped for a specific job, none of them pretending to be the others. That's closer to how these four APIs actually split up the work than any single ranked list.

shot.prompt: real photo of a multi-tool pocket knife fanned open, showing several distinct blades and implements -- illustrative of distinct tools built for different specific jobs, not a literal depiction of any model's capabilities. Already sourced, see media/A3-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push across the frame

beats.act: Act III — Built For What, Exactly
beats.narration_text: Anthropic's own stated focus: coding and agentic tool use, long-horizon reasoning, and enterprise deployment — Claude Code is the flagship expression of that bet.

beats.act: Act III — Built For What, Exactly
beats.narration_text: OpenAI's bet is breadth: the largest consumer surface in ChatGPT, the widest third-party plugin and tooling ecosystem, and Codex-branded variants purpose-built for coding specifically.

beats.act: Act III — Built For What, Exactly
beats.narration_text: Google's bet leans on what only Google has: native integration with Search, Workspace, and Android, plus multimodal input built in from the ground up, not bolted on after.

items: multimodal input from the ground up
props.caption: the ecosystem bet

beats.act: Act III — Built For What, Exactly
beats.narration_text: One API key gets you a managed endpoint, someone else's uptime, someone else's rate limits. Your own hardware gets you full control — and full responsibility for keeping it running.

data.question: One API key, or your own hardware?

resolver.label: Convenience, or control

beats.act: Act III — Built For What, Exactly
beats.narration_text: The open-weight bet is control: self-hostable for data-sovereignty-sensitive deployments, fine-tunable on your own data, and small enough variants to run as local, on-device agents.

items: self-hostable, data stays on your own infrastructure
small variants for local, on-device agents
props.caption: the control bet

beats.act: Act IV — Open Weights, Closed Weights, and Everything Between
beats.narration_text: Act four: open weights, closed weights, and everything between.

props.title: Open Weights, Closed Weights, and Everything Between

beats.act: Act IV — Open Weights, Closed Weights, and Everything Between
beats.narration_text: Locked, deliberately, with the mechanism visible right there in the door itself — nobody questions what this object is for. A closed-weight model works the same way: the design is intentional, not an oversight.

shot.prompt: real photo of a bank vault door's locking mechanism, bolts and handles visible -- illustrative of a closed, locked system, not a literal depiction of any model's weights. Already sourced, see media/A4-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push across the frame

beats.act: Act IV — Open Weights, Closed Weights, and Everything Between
beats.narration_text: The old split was clean: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all fully closed-weight, API-only. Meta stood alone as the one major lab still shipping open weights at real scale.

props.sparkLine: The split that used to exist.
items: Meta: the one major open-weight lab
props.caption: clean, and now out of date

beats.act: Act IV — Open Weights, Closed Weights, and Everything Between
beats.narration_text: That changed. Meta's own newest frontier model launched closed — their first proprietary, API-only release. At the same time, they shipped a genuinely open-weight model under Apache two-point-oh, a stronger license than their old one.

items: Meta's newest flagship launched closed, API-only — a first
a separate model shipped open-weight under Apache 2.0
props.caption: the same company, two licenses

beats.act: Act IV — Open Weights, Closed Weights, and Everything Between
beats.narration_text: Same company, same year, two different answers. The flagship: proprietary, API-only, closed weights. The smaller model, released days apart: open weights, Apache two-point-oh, download it and run it yourself.

show.event: two tracks diverge: closed flagship, open smaller release

beats.act: Act IV — Open Weights, Closed Weights, and Everything Between
beats.narration_text: Even the historical open-weight license carried an asterisk: free to use and modify, but a company above seven hundred million monthly users needed a separate commercial license from Meta directly.

items: free to use and modify, for almost everyone
companies over 700M monthly users: a separate license required
props.caption: source-available, not unconditionally open

beats.act: Act IV — Open Weights, Closed Weights, and Everything Between
beats.narration_text: Four companies, four real specializations, and a licensing map that got more interesting, not simpler. The actual question was never which one wins — it's which one fits the thing you're actually building.

items: the licensing map got messier, not simpler
the question was always: which fits your build
props.caption: not which wins. which fits

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. On cost, all three hyperscalers — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google — price their flagship models in the same rough band, two to ten dollars in, ten to fifty out, per million tokens; open-weight models like Meta's have no single price, because cost depends entirely on who hosts them. On context window, the race has converged — Claude, GPT, and Gemini flagships all cluster near one million input tokens now, and the real remaining differentiator is max output, generally capped near a hundred twenty-eight thousand. On use case, each company is actually making a different bet: Anthropic for coding and agentic work, OpenAI for ecosystem breadth, Google for native multimodal integration, and open-weight models for self-hosted, data-sovereign deployments. And on open versus proprietary, the clean split is gone — Meta's own twenty twenty-six lineup now runs both a closed frontier model and a true open-weight one under Apache two-point-oh, a stronger license than their old one.

show.event: four artifact lines stagger in, one per act

artifactLines: Cost: the three hyperscalers price flagships in the same rough band ($2-10 in / $10-50 out per MTok); open-weight models have no single price — it depends entirely on who hosts them.
Context window: the race converged — Claude, GPT, and Gemini flagships all cluster near 1M input tokens; the real differentiator now is max output (~128K) and how the window is counted.
Use case: each company is making a different bet — Anthropic for coding/agentic work, OpenAI for ecosystem breadth, Google for native multimodal integration, open weights for self-hosted control.
Open vs. proprietary: the clean split is gone — Meta's own 2026 lineup runs both a closed frontier model and a true open-weight one under Apache 2.0.
